questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why chocolate and sweets are bad for your health
How to live happily in a big city without a car
How supermarkets store and transport fresh milk
Putting carbon footprint labels on products
questions.why: Sam says they'll look at an idea to add a label showing the carbon footprint of a product.

questions.q: Why does Sam mention the label on Neil's chocolate bar?
options: To warn Neil about eating too much chocolate every day
As an example of a label that helps people compare products
To show that food labels are too small for people to read
To explain to listeners what a carbon footprint is
questions.why: The label shows sugar, fat and calories so consumers can compare the healthiness of things.

questions.q: What does Neil say about carbon labelling in the past?
options: It was very popular in British shops in the 1990s
It was banned by governments in most of Europe
It isn't a new idea, but it never became popular
It was only ever used for new cars and fuel
questions.why: Neil says it's not a new idea but it's something that has never caught on.

questions.q: According to Marc Engel, who is driving the demand for this information?
options: Younger shoppers like Gen Z
Governments and politicians in Europe
Supermarket managers
Environmental scientists
questions.why: He says Gen Z and Millennials are much more willing to make informed choices about responsible products.

questions.q: What does Marc Engel say about Unilever's reason for doing this?
options: It was an idea the company invented itself
It will make the products cheaper
It is required by law
They believe customers will ask for it
questions.why: He says they're doing it because this is what consumers will ask from business.

questions.q: How many products has Unilever promised to label?
options: 7 million
questions.why: Neil says Unilever committed to putting carbon information on 70,000 products.

questions.q: According to Dr Zaina Gadema-Cooke, why is it hard to measure a product's full carbon footprint?
options: Because people use and throw away products in different ways
Because farms and factories refuse to share their data
Because the labels are too expensive for shops to print
Because carbon can't be measured accurately by scientists
questions.why: She says it's almost impossible to include the consumer stage because we all use and dispose of products differently.

questions.q: What does Dr Gadema-Cooke mean when she says 'farm to fork' is really 'farm to retail shelf'?
options: Most food is wasted on farms before it reaches the shops
Calculations usually stop when the product reaches the shop
Shops and supermarkets add the most carbon to our food
Farmers are not included in the carbon calculations at all
questions.why: She says calculations tend to be 'farm-to-retail-shelf', as what happens after purchase is unknown.
